curves_matrix_description: Radius {radius}, smoothing {smoothing}. Each row is one curve, each column is one effect.
demo_state_compare_smoothing_off: The front collapses onto the back, so no red corners are visible.
demo_state_compare_smoothing_on: The four red wedges show how far the squircle pulls in from the CSS-rounded back.
demo_state_smoothing_off: Smoothing is off; the demo square uses standard CSS quarter-circle corners.
demo_state_smoothing_on: Smoothing is on; the demo square uses Lisse's squircle corners.
header_def_1: smooth to the hand; having no roughness anywhere on the surface
header_def_2: a of hair, sleek; lying flat, with no break in it (cheveux lisses).
header_def_3: fig. even, unbroken; carrying on without interruption.
header_def_b: of a curve or a line, running on without any sudden change of direction (une courbe lisse).
header_pronunciation_sr: Pronounced lees, adjective, from French lisse meaning smooth.
intro_lead: Lisse is a small JavaScript library that draws squircle corners, the same continuous curve Figma and iOS use. Bindings for React, Vue, and Svelte, plus a framework-agnostic core. Per-corner control, borders, and shadows are included.
meta_app_description: JavaScript library that draws squircle corners — the same continuous curve Figma and iOS use. Bindings for React, Vue, and Svelte, plus a framework-agnostic core. Per-corner control, borders, and shadows included.
meta_home_description: Squircle corners for the web. Bindings for React, Vue, and Svelte.
meta_playground_description: Tune radius, smoothing, curve type, borders, and shadows in your browser.
meta_what_description: Why squircles look softer than CSS border-radius, and how Lisse draws them.
playground_border_description: A border that follows the curve, in any of the usual CSS line styles.
playground_drop_shadow_description: A drop shadow traced from the exact same curve, so it hugs the shape at any radius.
playground_inner_shadow_description: An inset shadow that sits inside the curve — good for recessed or pressed surfaces.
section_capsule_desc: A radius bigger than the shape can fit clamps the corners into a smooth capsule.
section_cornershape_desc: Smoothing sets how softly the corner eases in — 0 is a plain arc, 1 a full squircle.
section_curvetype_desc: Pick the curve: Squircle (the Figma and iOS default), Arc (plain CSS border-radius), Superellipse (the new CSS corner-shape), or Clothoid (an extra-smooth blend).
section_percorner_desc: Give each corner its own radius and smoothing — handy for tabs, chips, and other lopsided shapes.
section_radius_desc: Drag to round the corners — at the maximum the box becomes a full circle.
what_p10_browser_support: So if you can find a setting of the CSS exponent that lands exactly on the shape sitting in your Figma file, you will have done something the people who tried the fit numerically could not. That setting does not appear to exist, though. It's hard to match a two-dimensional curve with one number, just as it's hard to describe a face by giving the width of the nose. It would be pretty easy to ship corner-shape everywhere tomorrow, for example, but Chrome, which added it in August 2025, is still ahead of Safari's flag and whatever Firefox is doing.
what_p11_lisse_fits: So Lisse draws the Figma curve as an SVG path and clips whatever element it wraps to that path. For borders, it strokes the same path rather than a new one. When shadows are drawn, the thing being blurred is an offset copy of the clip, which keeps the soft edge honest. You can't compose per-corner radii cleanly unless the joins are handled, and once they are, a soft corner can meet a sharp one without a kink.
what_p12_observer: Because redrawing costs something, the right time to do it is not on every frame, but only when the box an element occupies has actually changed size. One shared ResizeObserver handles the whole page.
what_p13_docs_pointer: A page of Bézier control points looks fairly impressive. (They are in the docs, along with the per-corner composition rules.) And there is a link to all of it at the bottom of this page.
what_p1_intro: There are worse problems in interface design than a corner. A more annoying one is that the corner is never quite right. Icons are where most people first noticed the difference. If you look at an iPhone home screen for long enough, there is a natural temptation to believe, for example, that the icons are just rounded rectangles with a large radius applied to them. All the time Apple has been shipping that shape, which is since iOS 7 landed in 2013, there has been a quiet feeling among designers that the corner is doing something a border-radius does not, and that it was faintly embarrassing not to be able to name it.
what_p2_border_radius: For example, the usual explanation is that a rounded corner ought to be a quarter of a circle, drawn at whatever radius the design calls for. That is exactly what border-radius does. It works by cutting an arc into the box and joining it to the two straight edges. Worse still, instead of easing gradually into that arc the way a road eases into a bend, the curvature goes from nothing at all to its full value across a single point, and stays there. At four or five pixels, this is a detail nobody has ever complained about or noticed. Somewhere past sixteen, the seam starts to show.
what_p3_two_shapes: For a long time there was no fix for this on the web, just as there was no way to ask a design tool for anything other than a plain circular corner. If you look over at the people who solved it elsewhere, the type designers or the road engineers, you find there is a name for what is missing: continuous curvature. As far as anyone can tell, there are only two shapes in common use that provide it. A superellipse leans between a circle and a square, and one exponent decides how far.
what_p4_apple_shape: While we're on the subject of shapes, the other one keeps a small circular arc at the apex of the corner and grows a shoulder on each side of it. The shoulders are what let the curvature arrive gradually instead of all at once. Apple uses this second one. At any rate, the result is that the two halves of an Apple corner are not quite mirror images. On a square icon this probably doesn't do much harm, but the further you get from a square, the more of a problem it becomes.
what_p5_apple_fixed: None of this is adjustable, which has real consequences. It means that the shape you get is, above all, fixed. There is a short straight segment on one side of the corner that should not be there. The people who extracted the path call it a bug. A fixed curve would be a fine idea if every element on a screen were shaped the way an app icon is. But that is not how any of the interfaces on a real screen are laid out. What is wanted is a curve you can turn down a little when the element is long and thin, not a curve that was cut once for a grid of square icons and then sealed into the operating system.
what_p6_figma_redraw: Figma hit this in 2018. The main reason they redrew the curve is that Apple's path is not a formula. It is a run of control points, tuned once and then preserved across releases by an accident of history, like a spelling. At one end you have people who trace the path out of the operating system directly, and match it exactly, asymmetry and all. In the middle you have people fitting something simpler over the top of it, a superellipse with a single exponent, for example, and getting close. And then at the other extreme you have Daniel Furse, who went looking for the idea behind the shape rather than the shape itself, and for whom the fit was a blind alley, as it turns out it is for everyone. The closest single exponent lands near five, and the error left over is systematic.
what_p7_smoothing_dial: Because Figma derived the corner rather than copied it, you can turn the smoothing up and down. If you run the dial from one end to the other, you'll find that zero gives back the plain quarter circle that CSS has always drawn. When there's a setting that works very well, it is usually around sixty per cent, which is close enough to an iPhone icon that nobody picks it out.
what_p8_css_catching_up: CSS is arriving at this from the other side. A working group at the W3C writes the rules that browsers agree to follow, and once something has been sitting in a draft long enough people stop noticing that a draft is not a browser. But for anyone shipping today this gap is a problem. The new property is called corner-shape, and it sits next to border-radius in the Borders 4 draft. So instead of tracing the quarter circle it has always traced, which is the only thing it could do before, the radius can be told to follow some other curve entirely.
what_p9_squircle_keyword: There is a squircle keyword too. It resolves to superellipse(2), which under the spec's own notation works out to an exponent of four. That is a Lamé curve, which is the first of the two shapes, not the second. You might reasonably expect the two to be interchangeable at small sizes, in case you have to put a chip and an icon on the same row. Apple, Figma and Lisse in fact all draw the arc with shoulders, and CSS does not.
